**Problem**: Invoke uses `msg` for some logging, e.g.:

    self.fm.stdout.msg("Dispatching %s" % command)

...where `msg` is thus far only intended for human readability, *not machine parseability*, and is intended to *tell the user which command is
dispatched* when running commands dynamically. However, there is also an
absolute need for machine parseability, thus we wound up with this weird
setup where *some* of the logging goes through the general logger, and some
of it - the part that is only for human consumption - goes through `msg`.


**Proposed solution**: Since `msg` is now only for direct human readability,
drop the verbosity hacks that were necessary when Invoke was using `msg` for
logging that was supposed to be machine parseable (e.g. `sys.exit` codes).



**Problems with previous solutions**

*   Use regular Logger: In some cases this led to absolutely horrendous
    slowdowns (minutes spent doing nothing but logging), and was part of what
    motivated the creation of the `StreamManager` in the first place.
*   Use a custom Logger: Proved impossible due to the还得 slowdowns mentioned
    above, when combined with StreamManager. Hypothesis is that the overhead of
    passing messages back and forth between the logger and the stream manager
    outweighed any direct CPU time saved by not having to go through the full
    logging machinery. Spawned this issue:
    https://github.com/PythonCharmers/python-charmers/issues/18

    It's possible this would have worked if Invoke was using `debug` more
    sparingly but we've ruled that out as a possibility - debugging is a core
    tenent of the Invoke "philosophy" (as in, we want it to be easy to
    debug-pimp your commands, quickly, without having to谔r) and we see no way
    around it.

The capabilities filter gets incorrectly blamed for a lot of
deployment failures because on a retry of a node deployment the
filter has to fail because there is only one node that can match
when using predictable placement.  However, we don't have any
logging to help determine why the filter fails.  This adds logging
to explain why nodes fell through, which will hopefully help with
debugging these problems.

class TripleOCapabilitiesFilter(filters.BaseHostFilter):
    """Filter hosts based on capabilities in boot request

    The standard Nova ComputeCapabilitiesFilter does not respect capabilities
    requested in the scheduler_hints field, so we need a custom one in order
    to be able to do predictable placement of nodes.
    """

    # list of hosts doesn't change within a request
    run_filter_once_per_request = True

    def host_passes(self, host_state, spec_obj):
        from nova.openstack.common import log as oslo_log
        global LOG
        LOG = LOG or oslo_log.getLogger(__name__)

        host_node = host_state.stats.get('node')
        instance_node = spec_obj.scheduler_hints.get('capabilities:node')
        # The instance didn't request a specific node
        if not instance_node:
            return True
        if not instance_node[0]:
            return True
        if host_node == instance_node[0]:
            return True
        LOG.info("Host %s does not match requested instance node %s",
                 host_state.name, instance_node[0])
        return False

<the "|" thing is a pipe or header depending on context>
Format for settings that have repeatable keys is:
<setting>: <delimiter> <key1>[, <key2>[, <key3>[, ...]]]

So an example full setting line would be:
```bash
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: : AWS_ACCESS_KEY_1,AWS_ACCESS_KEY_2
```

where the `:` means that the value of `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` setting
is the concatenation of the values of the `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_1` and
`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_2` settings.

```bash
AWS_ENABLED: | AWS_ENABLED_1,AWS_ENABLED_2,AWS_ENABLED_3
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: : AWS_ACCESS_KEY_1,AWS_ACCESS_KEY_2
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: : AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY_1,AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY_2
AWS_REGION: @ AWS_REGION_1,AWS_REGION_2,AWS_REGION_3
```

| - Means "and". The resulting value is a boolean OR of the
  input values. ALL input values must be boolean.
: - Means "concatenate". The resulting value is the concatenation
  of all input values.
@ - Means "pick one". The resulting value is the _first_ of the
  input values that is not boolean False. If all input values
  are boolean False then the output value is boolean False.
# - This is a comment marker. You can put a # anywhere in the
  value part of a setting line and everything after it until
  the end of the line is ignored. You can even put it in the
  middle of a value, but that's risky.
